title: The 2-Minute Rule: Six Saves on a Pharma Floor

facts_used.claim: The 2-minute rule is a short, deliberate pause at the point of work, right before you start and again after any break, handover, interruption or change. 'Two minutes' is a rule of thumb and what matters is the pause; on a repeat task with nothing different, the pause takes seconds.
facts_used.source: brief-v2.md, 'The rule (verified consensus)'; proportionality framing from the operations-director review (framing, not a statistic)

facts_used.claim: The rule adds to SOPs, permits, lockout, confined-space programs and engineering controls such as guards and interlocks, and never replaces them. It catches what the plan didn't anticipate.
facts_used.source: brief-v2.md, 'The rule (verified consensus)'; hierarchy-of-controls point from the safety-manager review

facts_used.claim: Run it as Stop · Look · Ask · Decide. Ask: What's different? What could hurt us? Checked or assumed? What if it goes wrong? Decide: Go, Fix it if safe, or Stop & get help. A fix must be one you are trained and authorized for and that is in your procedure; anything else is Stop & get help.
facts_used.source: brief-v2.md, 'The rule (verified consensus)'; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 (lockout applied by authorized employees); safety-manager and operations-director reviews

facts_used.claim: Most pauses end in Go. This is the brief's framing, not a statistic. No number is given, and the tick runs on screen are deliberately too many to count, so no catch rate is implied.
facts_used.source: brief-v2.md, 'What the user asked for'; site-lead review

facts_used.claim: Under 21 CFR 211.130(e), packaging and labeling facilities are inspected immediately before use (shown as an on-screen chip, not read aloud). The 2-minute rule is line clearance for people.
facts_used.source: 21 CFR 211.130(e); result-4.json citable_facts and packaging changeover/line-clearance task

facts_used.claim: Tablet-press setup and tooling changeover are not minor servicing, so lockout applies at main power and compressed air. A changeover found half-finished at handover, with no lock on, is a Stop & get help. Isolation is verified with a try-start before work, the tooling is counted, and before locks come off the tools are removed, the area is clear and affected people are told. Guards go back on and each interlock is tested before restart, followed by the normal start-up checks.
facts_used.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 ((d)(6) verification, (e) release from lockout, (f)(4) shift changes) and OSHA minor-servicing interpretations; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.212; brief-v2.md use case 2; result-4.json tablet-press task ('locked out at main power and compressed air'; 'Are the tooling count and the inspection sheet ready?') and changeover task ('each interlock tested before restart'); safety-manager and operations-director reviews

facts_used.claim: Before a powder charge into a reactor holding flammable solvent, the first check is inerting with oxygen confirmed low on the reading. Bonding and grounding with a monitored clamp (red/green earth indicator) and the specified conductive or dissipative liner are a second layer. A drum lifter is used instead of tipping by hand.
facts_used.source: result-4.json powder-charging task (first check 'Is the vessel inerted, with oxygen confirmed low on the reading, not assumed?'; standard controls) and drum-handling task ('drum lifter instead of tipping by hand'); NFPA 77; CCPS Process Safety Beacon, March 2025; brief-v2.md use case 3

facts_used.claim: Nitrogen has no color or smell, and the hazard of an inerted vessel is oxygen-poor air.
facts_used.source: U.S. CSB Safety Bulletin 2003-10-B, Hazards of Nitrogen Asphyxiation; brief-v2.md use case 4

facts_used.claim: Before anyone opens or leans into a nitrogen-inerted vessel (here a filter dryer opened between campaigns for inspection), authorized people positively isolate the nitrogen (blind or spool removed and locked, not just a valve closed). They test oxygen and solvent vapor at the opening with a bump-tested meter before air goes in, ventilate, retest, and issue the permit. The pause never replaces the permit: no permit, no Go.
facts_used.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146; result-4.json nitrogen-inerted vessel task (positive isolation; test at the opening; solvent/LEL readings; bumped monitor); brief-v2.md use case 4 ('for inspection'); safety-manager review (de-inerting order and who does the work)

facts_used.claim: Normal air is about 20.9% oxygen. Under 29 CFR 1910.146, oxygen-deficient air is below 19.5% and oxygen-enriched air is above 23.5%. The gauge's tinted band and its label 'O₂ 19.5–23.5%' show this range.
facts_used.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 definitions, via result-4.json citable_facts

facts_used.claim: Routine jams may be cleared under a site's minor-servicing method, with jam tools and interlocked guards, only where an alternative effective protection exists, and an emergency stop alone is not that protection. A jam that needs a reach-in the tool can't make calls for lockout of every energy source, including stored pneumatic energy. You lock out power and air, bleed trapped air to zero, then try START to verify before reaching in.
facts_used.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 ((a)(2)(ii), (d)(5), (d)(6)) and OSHA minor-servicing interpretations; result-4.json packaging-jam task ('Can I clear this with the guard closed or with a tool, or do I have to reach in?'; stored-energy dump valves) and citable fact on the minor-servicing letters; brief-v2.md use case 1

facts_used.claim: A visual glove check at each use finds visible damage such as a cut. Pinholes need a physical integrity (leak or pressure-decay) test, and a replacement glove is leak-tested before use. The isolator pressure display should read in range. Highly potent APIs act at very low doses.
facts_used.source: result-4.json isolator/RABS task (visual check at each use; pressure decay per ISO 14644-7; glove management programme) and HPAPI task; PQE Group, '3W of Glove Integrity Test'; site-lead and safety-manager reviews

facts_used.claim: Lockout covers chemical and thermal energy. Before you break a line after CIP, the CIP supply and pump are isolated first, and the local gauge then verifies the line. Pressure trapped between closed valves is relieved by waiting, venting and confirming zero (vent open, no flow) and cool-down. You stand to the side of the joint, not in front of it, in a face shield and chemical gloves.
facts_used.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147; brief-v2.md use case 5; result-4.json CIP/SIP task (isolation and LOTO of steam, CIP supply and pumps; face shield and chemical gloves) and line-break task (gauge or vent check confirms zero; position to the side)

facts_used.claim: Anyone, staff or contractor, can stop a job, even on a late batch, with no reprisal or blame. Stopping means stopping the job, not shutting down a running process outside procedure.
facts_used.source: brief-v2.md, 'The rule (verified consensus)' (real authority to stop without reprisal); safety-manager and site-lead reviews; CSB 2003-10-B (almost half of the nitrogen incidents involved contractors; not stated on screen)

facts_used.claim: Leaders come quickly, thank you, fix the cause and tell you what changed. The rule is not a check-the-box form, and what you catch goes through your usual reporting channels.
facts_used.source: brief-v2.md, 'The rule (verified consensus)'; safety-manager, operations-director and site-lead reviews

facts_used.claim: The six use cases are illustrative composites built from common pharma hazards, not real incidents.

scenes.purpose: Teach Stop · Look · Ask · Decide with the four questions and the three decisions, and build the question cards and decision buttons that every save reuses. Define 'Checked or assumed?' once: did you look or test it yourself, or are you guessing? Then set the boundary rule where the decision is defined, as a side-by-side contrast. Fix it only if you are trained and authorized and it is a step in your procedure (e.g. clip on a grounding clamp, or bleed air to zero or vent a line under your own lock). Stop & get help when there is no permit yet, when it is someone else's unfinished work, or when you are not authorized for the repair (e.g. a cut isolator glove, a faulty guard or interlock, opening a vessel). If you are not sure, or the fix doesn't work, Stop & get help.

scenes.purpose: Set the base rate: most pauses end like the routine Go, in seconds, and catches are a small minority, with no ratio implied. Define a save as a pause where a question catches a problem. scenes.purpose: Q1, What's different?, at a shift handover. The note and a look at the press show the guard open, the tooling half in and no lock on the power switch. The call is Stop & get help, because it is someone else's unfinished work. Your lead comes, thanks you and checks with the last shift. An authorized press setter, not you, then locks out the disconnect and the air, bleeds the air to zero, tries START (nothing moves), finishes the change and counts the tooling. The guard is closed, tools are out and the area is clear, the setter removes their own lock, the interlock is tested and the start-up checks are done, then Go. Prevented: starting a press with its tooling half in.

scenes.purpose: Pay off the series: three fixes and three calls for help, and all six end in Go once it's safe. The goal is a safe start, not a fast one, and catches are a small share of all pauses, with no ratio implied. The pause is good for people, product and the line. It makes work go right and is not a brake on it.

scenes.purpose: State the commitments plainly, as commitments, not conditions. Anyone, staff or contractor, can stop a job, even on a late batch, with no punishment and no blame. That means stopping the task: running processes are stopped only through operating procedures. Leaders come quickly, thank you, fix the cause and tell you what changed. The pause is not a form, and what you catch is reported through your usual channels so the system defect gets fixed.
